questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q(\sqrt{3},\,\frac{11}{2},\,-7)$ and parallel to $v=⟨1,\,1,\,-2⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$ 

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨\sqrt{3},\,\frac{11}{2},\,-7⟩.$ 

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{3},\,\frac{11}{2},\,-7⟩+t⟨1,\,1,\,-2⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(0,-2,-4)$ and $Q(5,0,1)$, as follows:

$$

$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
questions.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(4,0,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,-6,3⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $PA=7.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩)-⟨4,0,-1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨2,-6,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-6t,\,3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=7,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PA & =7 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =7 \\ |⟨2t,\,-6t,\,3t⟩| & =7 \\ \sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-6t)^{2}+(3t)^{2}} & =7 \\ \sqrt{49{t}^{2}} & =7 \\ \pm 7t & =7 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨4,0,-1⟩+⟨2,-6,3⟩=⟨6,-6,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨4,0,-1⟩-⟨2,-6,3⟩=⟨2,6,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(6,-6,2)$ and ${A}_{2}(2,6,-4).$

questions.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,1,1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,-1,5⟩.$ Find all the possible points $Q$ on that line such that $PQ=3\sqrt{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $Q$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OQ} & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩)-⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PQ=3\sqrt{3},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |\overset{\to }{PQ}| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+(-t)^{2}+(5t)^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{27{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \pm 3\sqrt{3}t & =3\sqrt{3} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{1}}=⟨1,1,1⟩+⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨2,0,6⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{2}}=⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨0,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${Q}_{1}(2,0,6)$ and ${Q}_{2}(0,2,-4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩)-⟨3,-2,3⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-2,1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=3,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =3 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =3 \\ |⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩| & =3 \\ \sqrt{(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \pm 3t & =3 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩+⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨1,-1,5⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩-⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨5,-3,1⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Segment
questions.problem:
The equation below describes all the points on the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(-6,2,-1)$ and $Q(-8,0,-1).$

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ a\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ b \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,c]
$$

What is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

and the vector equation of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=(-1)+(-2)+1=-2.
$$

questions.problem:
The equation below gives a parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(-1,1,3)$ and $Q(0,6,-1).$

$$
r(t)=a\,i+(5t+1)\,j+b\,k,\,t\in [c,1]
$$

What is $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(6\,j-k)-(-i+j+3\,k) \\  & =i+5\,j-4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=(-i+j+3\,k)+t(i+5\,j-4\,k)
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(-i+j+3\,k)+t(i+5\,j-4\,k) \\  & =(t-1)\,i+(5t+1)\,j+(3-4t)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=(t-1)+(3-4t)+0=2-3t.
$$

$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(-4\,i-3\,k)+t(-2\,i+2\,j-2\,k) \\  & =-(2t+4)\,i+2t\,j-(2t+3)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(j-3\,k)-(3\,i+2\,j-k) \\  & =-3\,i-j-2\,k\end{aligned}

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=(3\,i+2\,j-k)+t(-3\,i-j-2\,k)
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(3\,i+2\,j-k)+t(-3\,i-j-2\,k) \\  & =(3-3t)\,i+(2-t)\,j-(2t+1)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=(3-3t)+(2-t)+1=6-4t.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Segment
questions.problem:
The equation below describes all the points on the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(5,0,4)$ and $Q(-3,1,5).$

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ a \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ b\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,c]
$$

What is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

and the vector equation of the  line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=0+1+1=2.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(3,-1,7)$ and parallel to $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v},
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty)$ and $\mathbf{p}$ is the position vector of $P$.

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
canonical_examples.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(1,-1,2)$ and $Q(3,2,7).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v},
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty)$ and $\mathbf{p}$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(1,-1,2)$ and $Q(3,2,7),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,2,7⟩-⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,2,0)$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}= \langle -4,1,1 \rangle.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $PA=6\sqrt{2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,2,0⟩+t⟨-4,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \langle 1, 2, 0 \rangle + t \langle -4, 1, 1 \rangle
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,2,0⟩+t⟨-4,1,1⟩)-⟨1,2,0⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-4,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t,\,t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=6\sqrt{2},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PA & =6\sqrt{2} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =6\sqrt{2} \\ |⟨-4t,\,t,\,t⟩| & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{(-4t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{18{t}^{2}} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \pm 3t\sqrt{2} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ t & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 2$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨1,2,0⟩+2⟨-4,1,1⟩=⟨-7,4,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨1,2,0⟩-2⟨-4,1,1⟩=⟨9,0,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are $A_1(-7, 4, 2)$ and $A_2(9, 0, -2).$

canonical_examples.problem: Using $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}$ notation, find a parametrization of the line segment $\overline{PQ},$ where $P(-4,1,2)$ and $Q(-2,5,-1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(-2\,i+5\,j-k)-(-4\,i+j+2\,k) \\  & =2\,i+4\,j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v} 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{r} = (-4 \, \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 2\,\mathbf{k}) + t (2 \, \mathbf{i} + 4 \, \mathbf{j} - 3 \, \mathbf{k})
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overline{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(-4\,i+j+2\,k)+t(2\,i+4\,j-3\,k) \\  & =(2t-4)\,i+(4t+1)\,j+(2-3t)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$
